instructions: Translate each "en" text into the target language and put it in the "ka" field. Use "context" to choose the right meaning. Keep it natural and short; for vocab terms give the dictionary form. Leave the field empty if you are not sure. Do not change "key" or "en".

items.context: C1 v — To form an opinion from evidence rather than direct statements. Example: What can we infer from these figures?
C1 v — To form or make up something. Example: Women constitute half of the workforce.
C1 v — To get something from a source. Example: Many English words derive from Latin.
C1 v — To improve the quality or value of something. Example: Good lighting can enhance a room.
C1 v — To make it difficult for something to happen. Example: Bad weather hindered the rescue efforts.
C1 v — To publicly support an idea or policy. Example: She advocates free public transport.
C1 v — To examine something very carefully. Example: The contract was scrutinised by lawyers.
C1 v — To get or gain something. Example: Children acquire language naturally.
C1 v — To give an amount of money, time or resources for a purpose. Example: More funds were allocated to research.
C1 v — To expect something and prepare for it. Example: We didn't anticipate so many visitors.
C1 v — To make up for something bad or missing; to pay for loss. Example: Nothing can compensate for the loss of a loved one.
C1 v — To communicate an idea or feeling. Example: Her face conveyed her disappointment.
C1 v — To become worse. Example: His health deteriorated rapidly.
C1 v — To decide something is not worth considering; to remove from a job. Example: She dismissed the idea as unrealistic.
C1 v — To publicly approve or support something. Example: The plan was endorsed by the committee.
C1 v — To imagine something as a future possibility. Example: I can't envisage living anywhere else.
C1 v — To use something to get an advantage; to treat people unfairly. Example: We must exploit this opportunity. Workers were exploited.
C1 v — To guess possible causes or results without knowing the facts. Example: Experts speculate that prices will rise.
C1 v — To keep something going over time. Example: The economy cannot sustain this level of growth.
C1 n — A difference between things that should be the same. Example: There's a discrepancy between the two reports.
C1 n — The quality of being fair, reasonable or legal. Example: The legitimacy of the election was questioned.
C1 n — The force that keeps something developing. Example: The campaign is gaining momentum.
C1 n — An earlier action used as an example for later decisions. Example: The ruling sets an important precedent.
C1 n — A publicly stated opinion. Example: What's the government's stance on immigration?
C1 n — A balance between two things you cannot have at the same time. Example: There's a trade-off between speed and quality.
C1 adj — Probably not honest, true or good. Example: The claims are dubious at best.
C1 adj — Very great or intense; showing deep understanding. Example: The internet has had a profound effect on society.
C1 adj — Large in amount or importance. Example: A substantial number of people disagreed.
C1 adj — Small and not very important. Example: There was only a marginal improvement.
C1 adj — Existing everywhere. Example: The influence of social media is pervasive.
C1 adj — Likely to cause disagreement. Example: Immigration is a contentious issue.
C1 adj — Based on chance rather than reason. Example: The decision seemed completely arbitrary.
C1 adj — Easily influenced or harmed by something. Example: Older people are more susceptible to infection.
C1 adj — Real and able to be shown or measured. Example: The reforms have produced tangible results.
C1 n — Something that encourages a person to do something. Example: Tax incentives encourage companies to invest.
C1 n — Money given by a government to reduce costs. Example: Farmers receive subsidies for growing wheat.
C1 n — A person who starts and runs a business. Example: Young entrepreneurs are changing the tech industry.
C1 n — The variety of plants and animals in an area. Example: Rainforests have extraordinary biodiversity.
C1 n — The amount of carbon dioxide produced by a person or activity. Example: Flying less is the easiest way to reduce your carbon footprint.
C1 n — The reduction of something until little is left. Example: Ozone depletion has slowed since the 1990s.
C1 n — Action to reduce how harmful something is. Example: Climate mitigation requires cutting emissions.
C1 n — The process of more people moving to and living in cities. Example: Rapid urbanisation has put pressure on housing.
C1 n — A group of people in a population, such as an age group. Example: The app is popular with a younger demographic.
C1 adj — Treated as unimportant and excluded from society. Example: The project supports marginalised communities.
C1 adj — Rich. Example: They live in an affluent suburb.
C1 n — A large difference, often unfair. Example: There is a wide disparity between rural and urban incomes.
C1 n — The division of a group into opposing views. Example: Political polarisation has increased.
C1 adj — Relating to what is morally right. Example: The research raises ethical questions.
C1 n — The control of information, books or films that are considered unacceptable. Example: The government was accused of censorship.
C1 v — To begin (formal). Example: The ceremony will commence at noon.
C1 n — A serious attempt to achieve something (formal). Example: Despite our best endeavours, the project failed.
C1 adv — After something else happened (formal). Example: He was arrested and subsequently released.
C1 prep — Before (formal). Example: Please arrive 30 minutes prior to departure.
C1 phr — Following a rule or wish (formal). Example: The work was done in accordance with the regulations.
C1 phr — About; concerning (formal). Example: With regard to your complaint, we have issued a refund.
C1 adv — As a result of this action (formal). Example: They cut costs, thereby increasing profits.
C1 pv — To improve your knowledge of something you learned before. Example: I need to brush up on my French before the trip.
C1 pv — To find by chance; to seem to have particular qualities. Example: I came across an old photo. She comes across as very confident.
C1 pv — To fail to happen. Example: Our plans to buy the house fell through.
C1 pv — To solve small problems or difficulties. Example: We need to iron out a few details before signing.
C1 pv — To make something seem less important than it is. Example: The government tried to play down the crisis.
C1 pv — To choose one person or thing from a group for special attention. Example: She was singled out for praise.
C1 pv — To be caused by something. Example: Many of his problems stem from his childhood.
C1 pv — To leave an important job or position. Example: The CEO stepped down after the scandal.
C1 pv — To consider carefully the advantages and disadvantages. Example: You need to weigh up the pros and cons.
C1 pv — To explain; to form a particular amount of something. Example: How do you account for the drop in sales? Exports account for 40% of income.
C1 pv — To cause something to happen. Example: The internet has brought about huge social changes.
C1 pv — To use knowledge or experience to help you. Example: She drew on her years of experience.
C1 pv — To mention a subject briefly. Example: The lecture only touched on the issue of cost.
C1 pv — To be the main point of something. Example: The problem boils down to a lack of money.
C1 phr — Something with both good and bad effects. Example: Fame can be a double-edged sword.
C1 phr — A small, visible part of a much larger problem. Example: These cases are just the tip of the iceberg.
C1 phr — A situation that is not clearly defined or regulated. Example: The use of AI in exams is still a grey area.
C1 phr — To make more effort than is expected. Example: Our staff always go the extra mile for customers.
C1 phr — To do something cheaply or quickly by ignoring rules or quality. Example: The builders cut corners, and now the roof leaks.
C1 phr — To fail to understand the main idea. Example: You're missing the point: it's about safety, not cost.
C1 phr — To be unable to decide. Example: I'm in two minds about accepting the offer.
C1 phr — To correct a false story or belief. Example: I'd like to set the record straight about what happened.
C1 phr — In general; mostly. Example: By and large, the event was a success.
C1 phr — Something that makes you think seriously. Example: The documentary gave me food for thought.
C1 adv — Used when you think something is true but others may disagree. Example: She is arguably the best writer of her generation.
C1 adv — Used to accept that something is true, even if it weakens your argument. Example: Admittedly, the plan is expensive, but it will save money long-term.
C1 adv — Used to say that you think something is probably true. Example: Presumably, the train is delayed.
C1 conj — To the degree that. Example: The plan is useful insofar as it reduces costs.
C1 phr — Mostly; to a great degree. Example: Success depends to a large extent on timing.
C1 phr — A cautious way to introduce an opinion. Example: It could be argued that the policy has failed.
C1 phr — After considering all the facts. Example: On balance, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
C1 phr — Taking everything into account. Example: All things considered, the trip went well.
C1 v — To express ideas or feelings clearly in words. Example: She articulated the concerns of many staff.
C1 adj — Suggested but not directly expressed. Example: There was an implicit criticism in his remarks.
C1 adj — Clear and exact, leaving nothing to be guessed. Example: The instructions were explicit.
C1 adj — Belonging naturally to something as a basic part. Example: Art has an intrinsic value beyond money.
C1 adj — Based on clear thinking and reason. Example: There must be a rational explanation.
C1 n — A way of thinking based on reason. Example: I can't follow the logic of his argument.
C1 n — A basic rule or belief that explains how something works or how to behave. Example: The system is based on the principle of equality.
C1 n — The size, degree or importance of something. Example: To what extent do you agree?
C1 n — A series of events or things in a particular order. Example: Describe the sequence of events that led to the crash.
C1 n — The study of the nature of knowledge, reality and existence; also, a set of beliefs. Example: The company's philosophy is to put customers first.
C1 n — A set of beliefs, especially political ones. Example: The party has moved away from its traditional ideology.
C1 n — The quality of deserving respect. Example: Every person should be treated with dignity.
C1 n — Freedom from unfair control by authority. Example: They fought for liberty and justice.
C1 n — Good judgement based on knowledge and experience. Example: She shared the wisdom of her many years.
C1 v — To make an idea, feeling or structure stronger. Example: The results reinforce the need for change.
C1 v — To make something, especially something bad, continue. Example: Such films perpetuate harmful stereotypes.
C1 v — To officially force a rule, tax or punishment on people. Example: The government imposed new restrictions.
C1 v — To keep or continue to have something. Example: The company struggles to retain good staff.
C1 v — To take something out or back; to stop taking part. Example: He withdrew from the competition.
C1 v — To separate something or someone from others. Example: Scientists isolated the gene responsible.
C1 v — To be greater than a number or amount. Example: Demand far exceeded supply.
C1 adv — Certainly; without doubt. Example: She is undoubtedly the best candidate.
C1 adj — Real and exactly what it seems to be; sincere. Example: He showed genuine concern for others.
C1 adj — Honest and direct, even when this is unpleasant. Example: Let me be frank: the plan won't work.
C1 adj — Seeming real or true, but perhaps not; also, easy to see. Example: For no apparent reason, the meeting was cancelled.
C1 adj — Used to emphasise how small or unimportant something is. Example: The tickets sold out in a mere ten minutes.
C1 n — The money used in a particular country. Example: The local currency fell against the dollar.
C1 n — The management of large amounts of money; money needed for a project. Example: She works in corporate finance.
C1 n — A situation in which there is not enough of something. Example: There is a shortage of skilled workers.
C1 n — An official plan or system. Example: The government launched a scheme to help first-time buyers.
C1 n — The buying and selling of goods and services, especially between countries. Example: Trade between the two countries has doubled.
C1 n — The protection of nature, buildings or resources. Example: The charity works on wildlife conservation.
C1 n — Something that is dangerous. Example: Air pollution is a serious health hazard.
C1 n — The natural home of an animal or plant. Example: Deforestation is destroying the orangutan's habitat.
C1 n — The state of people or parts being united and working well together. Example: The policy aims to strengthen social cohesion.
C1 n — Someone's social or professional position; the situation at a particular time. Example: Teachers have high status in Finland.
C1 n — A change that improves a system or institution. Example: The government promised education reform.
C1 n — A sudden and complete change, especially in politics or technology. Example: The internet caused a revolution in communication.
C1 n — Something you must do because of a law, promise or duty. Example: Employers have a legal obligation to ensure safety.
C1 v — To allow something officially. Example: Smoking is not permitted in the building.
C1 v — To formally give a document or proposal to someone in authority. Example: Applications must be submitted by 30 June.
C1 v — To put a name or information on an official list. Example: You must register with a doctor.
C1 v — To tell someone facts or information, especially officially. Example: Please inform us of any changes.
C1 n — A part of a whole, or the relationship between two amounts. Example: A large proportion of students work part-time.
C1 adj — Extremely good or impressive. Example: The book has been a phenomenal success.
C1 adv — Especially; in a way that deserves attention. Example: Several countries, notably Germany, have changed the law.
C1 phr — Used to express the basic or most important point. Example: In essence, the plan is about saving money.
C1 n — A disadvantage or problem. Example: The main drawback of the plan is its cost.
C1 v — To stop happening or existing. Example: The company ceased trading in 2020.
C2 adj — Clear, logical and convincing. Example: She presented a cogent case for reform.
C2 adj — Very weak or slight, and easily challenged. Example: The link between the two events is tenuous at best.
C2 n — An opinion expressed in an argument; also, disagreement. Example: It is my contention that the policy has failed.
C2 n — Language intended to persuade or impress, often without real substance. Example: Behind the rhetoric, little has actually changed.
C2 adj — Used for effect rather than to get information or express a real meaning. Example: It was a rhetorical question; he didn't expect an answer.
C2 n — The ability to speak or write fluently and persuasively. Example: Her eloquence won over even her critics.
C2 adj — Expressing ideas clearly and persuasively. Example: He gave an eloquent defence of free speech.
C2 n — The act of making someone believe or do something by giving reasons. Example: It took a lot of persuasion to change his mind.
C2 v — To prove that a statement or theory is wrong. Example: The scientist refuted the claim with new data.
C2 v — To provide evidence that something is true. Example: The allegations have not been substantiated.
C2 v — To support a statement or theory with additional evidence. Example: Two witnesses corroborated her account.
C2 v — To explain something clearly so that it is easier to understand. Example: The author elucidates a complex theory in simple terms.
C2 n — An idea or statement on which an argument is based. Example: The whole argument rests on a false premise.
